questions.question: A `UserManager` class validates user data, saves users to a file, AND sends welcome emails. Which principle does this violate?
questions.explanation: Three unrelated responsibilities (validation, persistence, email) bundled into one class means three unrelated reasons for it to change — a textbook SRP violation. Split it into three focused classes.

questions.question: Which change best demonstrates the Open/Closed Principle?
options: Adding an `if (shape is Triangle)` branch to an existing Area() method
Adding a new `Triangle : Shape` class with its own `override Area()`, without touching any existing code
Deleting the Shape base class and starting over
questions.explanation: OCP means extending behavior by ADDING new code (a new subclass), not modifying working, already-tested code with more branches. Polymorphism is what makes this possible.

questions.question: Why does `Square : Rectangle` (where setting Width also silently changes Height) violate LSP?
options: Code written correctly against Rectangle's documented behavior breaks when handed a Square instead, because Square secretly changes what setting Width means
Square should inherit from Circle instead
It doesn't violate anything, this is fine
questions.explanation: LSP requires that any subclass can be substituted for its base type without surprising behavior. A Square silently coupling Width and Height breaks reasonable expectations set by Rectangle, so substituting one for the other produces wrong results.

questions.question: A `RobotWorker` is forced to implement `Eat()` from a fat `IWorker` interface, even though robots don't eat, and just throws `NotImplementedException`. Which principle fixes this?
options: Interface Segregation — split IWorker into smaller, focused interfaces like IWorkable and IFeedable
questions.explanation: ISP says don't force implementers to provide methods they don't need. Splitting the fat interface into focused ones lets RobotWorker implement only IWorkable, with no irrelevant stub methods.

questions.question: What does this refactor demonstrate?
options: Dependency Inversion — depending on an interface (INotifier) instead of a concrete class, injected via constructor
This is not a SOLID-related change
questions.explanation: This is DIP in action: OrderProcessor no longer creates its own concrete EmailSender; it depends on an abstraction (INotifier) that's handed to it from outside — constructor (dependency) injection.

questions.question: Constructor (dependency) injection, which you'll use constantly in ASP.NET Core, is a direct application of the Dependency Inversion Principle.
questions.explanation: Exactly — ASP.NET Core's DI container exists specifically to supply constructors with interface implementations from the outside, instead of classes constructing their own dependencies internally.
